Computer [operating systems](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") (OSes) provide a set of functions needed and used by most application programs on a computer, and the links needed to control and synchronize computer hardware. On the first computers, with no operating system, every program needed the full hardware specification to run correctly and perform standard tasks, and its own drivers for [peripheral](/wiki/Peripheral "Peripheral") devices like printers and [punched paper card readers](/wiki/Punched_card "Punched card"). The growing complexity of hardware and application programs eventually made operating systems a necessity for everyday use.

title: History of operating systems
text:
Early computers lacked any form of operating system. Instead, the user (rarely also the computer operator), had sole use of the machine for a scheduled period of time. The user would deliver his program to a computer operator who would be responsible for loading the computer with the program and data needed for its 'run'.

Eventually, the end of a user's program could be detected and a control program automatically loaded which would load the next user's program, relieving the operator of having to load in each user's program individually and introducing the era of 'batched' programming. That is, a number of user programs could all be loaded together in a batch. Loading of program and data was accomplished in various ways including toggle switches (only used by a user on the earliest of computers, but later used by the computer operator to control the computer, e.g., to start it up, to shut it down, to 'pause', to 'dump' its RAM contents, and/or to control its input and/or its output), punched paper cards and magnetic or paper tape.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Once loaded, the machine would be set to execute each program singly until that program completed, crashed, exceeded its time limit or went into a(n infinite) loop. In those early days, there were only 'Control Program' units for providing the software necessary to control the computers and ancillary hardware, e.g., for such semi hardware functions as I/O . None of the early 'Control Programs' were sufficiently sophisticated to recognize a looping user program or initiate a recovery action.

In those early days, there were only 'Control Program' units for providing the software necessary to control the computers and ancillary hardware, e.g., for such semi hardware functions as I/O . None of the early 'Control Programs' were sufficiently sophisticated to recognize a looping user program or initiate a recovery action.

Detection and recovery from a looping program was another critical operator function and was usually detected by the sound of the looping computer, whereupon the operator would simply initiate a complete dump of the executing program (for later debugging by the programmer) and then load in (or instruct the computer to go on to) the next user's program. Programs could sometimes be debugged via a control panel using dials, toggle switches and panel lights, making it a very manual and error-prone process.[[4]](#cite_note-4) But, this was quite rare, since the high cost of even the simplest of the early computers prohibited such exclusive use of a computer by an individual programmer. Almost all program debugging was done away from any computer by the original programmer perusing the program and the dump of its execution obtained, e.g., by the computer operator or automatically by some computer hardware exception detection (such as a timeout, an attempt to divide by zero, or an over or underflow). Programmers then could only very rarely have more than one computer 'run' per day!

[Assemblers](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language")[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) and [compilers](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler") were developed for programmers to translate program [source code](/wiki/Source_code "Source code") written in a symbolic language into [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code") that previously would have been hand-encoded. Later machines came with libraries of support code on punched cards or magnetic tape, which would be linked to the user's program to assist in operations such as input and output. This was the genesis of the modern-day operating system; however, machines still ran a single program or job at a time. At [Cambridge University](/wiki/Cambridge_University "Cambridge University") in England the job queue was at one time a string from which tapes attached to corresponding job tickets were hung with stationery pegs.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

title: History of operating systems
text:
## Mainframes

The first operating system used for real work was [GM-NAA I/O](/wiki/GM-NAA_I/O "GM-NAA I/O"), produced in 1956 by [General Motors](/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors")' Research division[[9]](#cite_note-9) for its [IBM 704](/wiki/IBM_704 "IBM 704").[[10]](#cite_note-CHM-1956-SW-10)[*[specify](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")*] Most other early operating systems for IBM mainframes were also produced by customers.[[11]](#cite_note-bozemanlugHistoryOfLinux-11)

Early operating systems were very diverse, with each vendor or customer producing one or more operating systems specific to their particular [mainframe computer](/wiki/Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer"). Every operating system, even from the same vendor, could have radically different models of commands, operating procedures, and such facilities as debugging aids. Typically, each time the manufacturer brought out a new machine, there would be a new operating system, and most applications would have to be manually adjusted, recompiled, and retested.

title: History of operating systems
text:
### Systems on IBM hardware

Main article: [History of IBM mainframe operating systems](/wiki/History_of_IBM_mainframe_operating_systems "History of IBM mainframe operating systems")

Building on customer experience and requirements, IBM took on a more active role in developing operating systems for the [709](/wiki/IBM_709 "IBM 709"), [1410](/wiki/IBM_1410 "IBM 1410"), [7010](/wiki/IBM_7010 "IBM 7010"), [7040](/wiki/IBM_7040 "IBM 7040"), [7044](/wiki/IBM_7044 "IBM 7044"), [7090](/wiki/IBM_7090 "IBM 7090") and [7094](/wiki/IBM_7094 "IBM 7094"). IBM also collaborated with universities.

The state of affairs continued until the mid 1960s when [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), already a leading hardware vendor, stopped work on existing systems and put all its effort into developing the [System/360](/wiki/IBM_System/360 "IBM System/360") series of machines, all of which used the *same* instruction and input/output architecture. IBM intended to develop a single operating system for the new hardware, the [OS/360](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors"). The problems encountered in the development of the OS/360 are legendary, and are described by [Fred Brooks](/wiki/Fred_Brooks "Fred Brooks") in *[The Mythical Man-Month](/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month "The Mythical Man-Month")*—a book that has become a classic of [software engineering](/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering"). Because of performance differences across the hardware range and delays with software development, a whole family of operating systems was introduced instead of a single OS/360.[[12]](#cite_note-JohnsonVSEPast40Years-12)[[13]](#cite_note-Boyer360Revolution-13)

Because of performance differences across the hardware range and delays with software development, a whole family of operating systems was introduced instead of a single OS/360.[[12]](#cite_note-JohnsonVSEPast40Years-12)[[13]](#cite_note-Boyer360Revolution-13)

IBM wound up releasing a series of stop-gaps followed by two longer-lived operating systems:

- [OS/360](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors") for mid-range and large systems. This was available in three [system generation](/wiki/System_Generation_(OS) "System Generation (OS)") options:
  - [PCP](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#PCP "OS/360 and successors") for early users and for those without the resources for multiprogramming.
  - [MFT](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#MFT "OS/360 and successors") for mid-range systems, replaced by MFT-II in OS/360 Release 15/16. This had one successor, [OS/VS1](/wiki/OS/VS1 "OS/VS1"), which was discontinued in the 1980s.
  - [MVT](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#MVT "OS/360 and successors") for large systems. This was similar in most ways to PCP and MFT (most programs could be ported among the three without being [re-compiled](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler")), but has more sophisticated memory management and a [time-sharing](/wiki/Time-sharing "Time-sharing") facility, [TSO](/wiki/Time_Sharing_Option "Time Sharing Option"). MVT had several successors including the current [z/OS](/wiki/Z/OS "Z/OS").

### Other mainframe operating systems

[Control Data Corporation](/wiki/Control_Data_Corporation "Control Data Corporation") developed the [SCOPE](/wiki/CDC_SCOPE "CDC SCOPE") operating systems[[NB 1]](#cite_note-15) in the 1960s, for [batch processing](/wiki/Batch_processing "Batch processing") and later developed the [MACE](/wiki/CDC_Kronos "CDC Kronos") operating system for time sharing, which was the basis for the later [Kronos](/wiki/CDC_Kronos "CDC Kronos"). In cooperation with the [University of Minnesota](/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), the Kronos and later the [NOS](/wiki/NOS_(operating_system) "NOS (operating system)") operating systems were developed during the 1970s, which supported simultaneous batch and time sharing use. Like many commercial time sharing systems, its interface was an extension of the [DTSS](/wiki/Dartmouth_Time-Sharing_System "Dartmouth Time-Sharing System") time sharing system, one of the pioneering efforts in timesharing and programming languages.

In the late 1970s, Control Data and the [University of Illinois](/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Urbana%E2%80%93Champaign "University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign") developed the [PLATO system](/wiki/PLATO_(computer_system) "PLATO (computer system)"), which used plasma panel displays and long-distance time sharing networks. PLATO was remarkably innovative for its time; the shared memory model of PLATO's [TUTOR programming language](/wiki/TUTOR_(programming_language) "TUTOR (programming language)") allowed applications such as real-time chat and multi-user graphical games.

title: History of operating systems
text:
## Minicomputers

Digital Equipment Corporation created several operating systems for its 16-bit [PDP-11](/wiki/PDP-11 "PDP-11") machines, including the simple [RT-11](/wiki/RT-11 "RT-11") system, the time-sharing [RSTS](/wiki/RSTS/E "RSTS/E") operating systems, and the [RSX-11](/wiki/RSX-11 "RSX-11") family of [real-time operating systems](/wiki/Real-time_operating_system "Real-time operating system"), as well as the [VMS](/wiki/OpenVMS "OpenVMS") system for the 32-bit [VAX](/wiki/VAX "VAX") machines.

Several competitors of Digital Equipment Corporation such as [Data General](/wiki/Data_General "Data General"), [Hewlett-Packard](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard"), and [Computer Automation](/wiki/Computer_Automation "Computer Automation") created their own operating systems. One such, "MAX III", was developed for [Modular Computer Systems](/wiki/MODCOMP "MODCOMP") Modcomp II and Modcomp III computers. It was characterised by its target market being the industrial control market. The Fortran libraries included one that enabled access to measurement and control devices.

Several competitors of Digital Equipment Corporation such as [Data General](/wiki/Data_General "Data General"), [Hewlett-Packard](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard"), and [Computer Automation](/wiki/Computer_Automation "Computer Automation") created their own operating systems. One such, "MAX III", was developed for [Modular Computer Systems](/wiki/MODCOMP "MODCOMP") Modcomp II and Modcomp III computers. It was characterised by its target market being the industrial control market. The Fortran libraries included one that enabled access to measurement and control devices.

IBM's key innovation in operating systems in this class (which they call "mid-range"), was their "CPF" for the [System/38](/wiki/IBM_System/38 "IBM System/38"). This had [capability-based addressing](/wiki/Capability-based_addressing "Capability-based addressing"), used a machine interface architecture to isolate the application software and most of the operating system from hardware dependencies (including even such details as address size and register size) and included an integrated [RDBMS](/wiki/Relational_database_management_system "Relational database management system"). The succeeding OS/400 (now known as [IBM i](/wiki/IBM_i "IBM i")) for the [IBM AS/400](/wiki/IBM_AS/400 "IBM AS/400") and later [IBM Power Systems](/wiki/IBM_Power_Systems "IBM Power Systems") has no files, only objects of different types and these objects persist in very large, flat virtual memory, called a single-level store.

The [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") operating system was developed at AT&T Bell Laboratories in the late 1960s, originally for the [PDP-7](/wiki/PDP-7 "PDP-7"), and later for the PDP-11. Because it was essentially free in early editions, easily obtainable, and easily modified, it achieved wide acceptance. It also became a requirement within the Bell systems operating companies. Since it was written in the [C language](/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)"), when that language was ported to a new machine architecture, Unix was also able to be ported. This portability permitted it to become the choice for a second generation of minicomputers and the first generation of [workstations](/wiki/Workstation "Workstation"), and its use became widespread. Unix exemplified the idea of an operating system that was conceptually the same across various hardware platforms. Because of its utility, it inspired many and later became one of the roots of the [free software](/wiki/Free_software "Free software") movement and [open-source software](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software"). Numerous operating systems were based upon it including [Minix](/wiki/Minix "Minix"), [Linux](/wiki/History_of_Linux "History of Linux"), and the [Berkeley Software Distribution](/wiki/Berkeley_Software_Distribution "Berkeley Software Distribution"). Apple's [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") is also based on Unix via [NeXTSTEP](/wiki/NeXTSTEP "NeXTSTEP")[[15]](#cite_note-18) and [FreeBSD](/wiki/FreeBSD "FreeBSD").[[16]](#cite_note-19)

## Microcomputers

Beginning in the mid-1970s, a new class of small computers came onto the marketplace. Featuring 8-bit processors, typically the [MOS Technology 6502](/wiki/MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502"), [Intel 8080](/wiki/Intel_8080 "Intel 8080"), [Motorola 6800](/wiki/Motorola_6800 "Motorola 6800") or the [Zilog Z80](/wiki/Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80"), along with rudimentary input and output interfaces and as much [RAM](/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") as practical, these systems started out as kit-based hobbyist computers but soon evolved into an essential business tool.

title: History of operating systems
text:
### Home computers

While many eight-bit [home computers](/wiki/Home_computer "Home computer") of the 1980s, such as the [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro"), [Commodore 64](/wiki/Commodore_64 "Commodore 64"), [Apple II](/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"), [Atari 8-bit computers](/wiki/Atari_8-bit_computers "Atari 8-bit computers"), [Amstrad CPC](/wiki/Amstrad_CPC "Amstrad CPC"), [ZX Spectrum](/wiki/ZX_Spectrum "ZX Spectrum") series and others could load a third-party disk-loading operating system, such as [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") or [GEOS](/wiki/GEOS_(8-bit_operating_system) "GEOS (8-bit operating system)"), they were generally used without one. Their built-in operating systems were designed in an era when [floppy disk drives](/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk") were very expensive and not expected to be used by most users, so the standard storage device on most was a [tape drive](/wiki/Tape_drive "Tape drive") using standard [compact cassettes](/wiki/Compact_Cassette "Compact Cassette"). Most, if not all, of these computers shipped with a built-in [BASIC](/wiki/BASIC "BASIC") interpreter on ROM, which also served as a crude [command-line interface](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface"), allowing the user to load a separate [disk operating system](/wiki/Disk_operating_system "Disk operating system") to perform [file management](/wiki/File_management "File management") commands and load and save to disk.

On this hardware, a complex operating system's [overhead](/wiki/Overhead_(computing) "Overhead (computing)") supporting multiple tasks and users would likely compromise the performance of the machine without really being needed. As those systems were largely sold complete, with a fixed hardware configuration, there was also no need for an operating system to provide drivers for a wide range of hardware to abstract away differences.

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Apple_Lisa_%28Little_Apple_Museum%29_%288032162544%29.jpg/250px-Apple_Lisa_%28Little_Apple_Museum%29_%288032162544%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Apple_Lisa_(Little_Apple_Museum)_(8032162544).jpg)

Apple Lisa running Lisa OS

The development of microprocessors made inexpensive computing available for the [small business](/wiki/Small_business "Small business") and hobbyist, which in turn led to the widespread use of interchangeable hardware components using a common interconnection (such as the [S-100](/wiki/S-100_bus "S-100 bus"), SS-50, [Apple II](/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"), [ISA](/wiki/Industry_Standard_Architecture "Industry Standard Architecture"), and [PCI](/wiki/Conventional_PCI "Conventional PCI") [buses](/wiki/Bus_(computing) "Bus (computing)")), and an increasing need for "standard" operating systems to control them. The most important of the early OSes on these machines was [Digital Research](/wiki/Digital_Research "Digital Research")'s [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M")-80 for the 8080 / 8085 / Z80 CPUs. It was based on several Digital Equipment Corporation operating systems, mostly for the PDP-11 architecture. Microsoft's first operating system, [MDOS/MIDAS](/wiki/Marc_McDonald "Marc McDonald"), was designed along many of the PDP-11 features, but for microprocessor based systems. [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS"), or [PC DOS](/wiki/IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS") when supplied by IBM, was designed to be similar to CP/M-80.[[18]](#cite_note-21) Each of these machines had a small boot program in ROM which loaded the OS itself from disk. The BIOS on the IBM-PC class machines was an extension of this idea and has accreted more features and functions in the 20 years since the first IBM-PC was introduced in 1981.

## Rise of virtualization

Operating systems originally ran directly on the hardware itself and provided services to applications, but with virtualization, the operating system itself runs under the control of a [hypervisor](/wiki/Hypervisor "Hypervisor"), instead of being in direct control of the hardware.

On mainframes IBM introduced the notion of a [virtual machine](/wiki/Virtual_machine "Virtual machine") in 1968 with [CP/CMS](/wiki/CP/CMS "CP/CMS") on the [IBM System/360 Model 67](/wiki/IBM_System/360_Model_67 "IBM System/360 Model 67"), and extended this later in 1972 with [Virtual Machine Facility/370](/wiki/VM_(operating_system) "VM (operating system)") (VM/370) on [System/370](/wiki/IBM_System/370 "IBM System/370").

On [x86](/wiki/X86 "X86")-based [personal computers](/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer"), [VMware](/wiki/VMware "VMware") popularized this technology with their 1999 product, [VMware Workstation](/wiki/VMware_Workstation "VMware Workstation"),[[19]](#cite_note-22) and their 2001 VMware GSX Server and VMware ESX Server products.[[20]](#cite_note-23) Later, a wide range of products from others, including [Xen](/wiki/Xen "Xen"), [KVM](/wiki/Kernel-based_Virtual_Machine "Kernel-based Virtual Machine") and [Hyper-V](/wiki/Hyper-V "Hyper-V") meant that by 2010 it was reported that more than 80 percent of enterprises had a virtualization program or project in place, and that 25 percent of all server workloads would be in a virtual machine.[[21]](#cite_note-24)

Over time, the line between virtual machines, monitors, and operating systems was blurred:
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > History of operating systems

title: History of operating systems
text:
- Hypervisors grew more complex, gaining their own application programming interface,[[22]](#cite_note-25) memory management or file system.[[23]](#cite_note-26)
- Virtualization becomes a key feature of operating systems, as exemplified by [KVM](/wiki/Kernel-based_Virtual_Machine "Kernel-based Virtual Machine") and [LXC](/wiki/LXC "LXC") in Linux, [Hyper-V](/wiki/Hyper-V "Hyper-V") in [Windows Server 2008](/wiki/Windows_Server_2008 "Windows Server 2008") or [HP Integrity Virtual Machines](/wiki/HP_Integrity_Virtual_Machines "HP Integrity Virtual Machines") in [HP-UX](/wiki/HP-UX "HP-UX").
- In some systems, such as [POWER5](/wiki/POWER5 "POWER5") and later POWER servers from IBM, the hypervisor is no longer optional.[[24]](#cite_note-27)
- Radically simplified operating systems, such as [CoreOS](/wiki/CoreOS "CoreOS") have been designed to run only on virtual systems.[[25]](#cite_note-28)
- Applications have been re-designed to run directly on a virtual machine monitor.[[26]](#cite_note-29)

In many ways, virtual machine software today plays the role formerly held by the operating system, including managing the hardware resources (processor, memory, I/O devices), applying scheduling policies, or allowing system administrators to manage the system.
